utterances.text: No, please I have to answer this. My course of action - I have to answer this - was to focus my energy on the area where we're talking because there was sufficient food there to feed these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So when you say there was sufficient food you saw the stocks of food?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that there was -- for example, a large humanitarian shipment of food on an ongoing basis from the Republic of Ireland to an area not too far from where we're talking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And you're saying that the municipality, this particular municipality, was denying that access to that food?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You know that for a fact?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked for food for these people and it was denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, did you talk to the mayor of that town or did you talk to the president of that municipality; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You talked to them.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did you try to learn what was available in their budget in order to provide assistance to these people?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. This was not a detention camp. There was where refugees were being put in; right? I'm not saying that --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: From where.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- this was a deluxe hotel.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My God, from where you're standing now, that's some comment. Let me tell you, let me tell you something. You have never experienced a place like this, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, did you visit other places around country to see where refugees were being placed as they came in?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm not talking about where they eventually ended up in and I'm not talking about as the war progresses or as this conflict progresses where there's time to find facilities.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say there is no excuse for housing people like that in that kind of state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ask what budget was available to them, if they had the budgetary means?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know what the budgetary means was at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. I won't press.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me share with you a document. It's dated 28 November 1992. This has to do with a slightly different matter. So it's 1D 01053. 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it here, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see that this is -- if you go to the second page --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to read this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please just do as I'm asking you to, and then if I'm unfair you can ask leave from the Trial Chamber for a fair treatment?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask the witness be allowed to read the document. He could have been supplied the document during the break and we could have saved time rather than playing these sorts of games. But the witness ought to be allowed to read the document before he's questioned about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking the gentleman just to look at the signature first. It's step by step and I don't see why Mr. Stringer got off the wrong side of the bed today. You know, he finished his direct, he must have had a nice meal last night with a glass of wine and relaxed. There is no need to be aggressive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, you know this is an outrageous comment to make in a courtroom in an international criminal tribunal. This sort of -- this sort of statement demeans all of us, myself, he demeaned me, he insulted me yesterday. He's doing it again. He drags us all down when he acts like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I merely said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, please keep calm. You're showing the witness a document which he's not familiar with. You're asking him to look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I wish to add, Mr. Karnavas, please refrain from these personal attacks and ironic remarks. They indeed throw venom in the atmosphere of the court and are completely unnecessary and let me add unprofessional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. -- Judge Trechsel. There's no need to correct me on that because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It seems there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you go back, Judge Trechsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We're not going to discuss this, Mr. Karnavas. This is so obvious. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The objection, in my opinion, was wrong. I'm entitled to do my cross-examination as I see fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But you're not entitled to make personal comments and attack persons personally, and that's what you've been doing several times and I do ask you to stop this because this is not professional. You can make all the objections you make. You can protest everything, but do not make these personal comments which are unprofessional, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I merely stated there's no need to get excited. That's all. That's how I started, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we -- can you please look at the signature line.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. See, there was no -- no way I was trying to mislead you with that question.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now it says "Prim". Do you know what that means, "Prim Dr.", what that stands for?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primary Dr., Orthopaedic -- I'm not sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's a title that they give to doctors in Bosnia-Herzegovina or that region that have attained a certain status within their profession, you know?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now if we can go back and if before we go to this document, who was this individual? You see we're going to do step-by-step there's no need to get excited in this courtroom. Who is this guy? You said you know him. Who is he?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This man was the -- the person in charge of this hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. At the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you had -- that's a yes?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you had an opportunity to meet with him?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Talk to him?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, did he by any chance inform you that he was receiving aid from abroad?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he mentioned that he was receiving some aid, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this letter is dated October 28 -- I mean, November 28, 1992. That would have been about the time that you were there; right?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you would take some time and look over the document now that we've set the foundation and we know that you know this individual so I'm trying to be fairer to you.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Contrary to what you know has been shown otherwise, if you could just look at the document, read it. I just have a couple of questions on this, that's all.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So can I read the document now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: See, we're going to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave if I may consult with my client while the gentleman is reading the letter. Just to get instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, while he reads the letter. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I'm told -- have you had a chance to read this?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, it's -- thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, it would appear at least there's a reference to Chetniks. You understand that means, right, what he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who is he referring to?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he is talking about the assistance that they're receiving and the assistance that he wishes; right?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's a yes?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I'm told by my client that there's one section that was not translated that might require a little bit of -- for my client to stand up and read it, because you can even see it in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic, apparently there is a section that hasn't been translated, so read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slow down -- slow. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: At the end of first page I am reading now Croat language: "[Interpretation] The food is almost more necessary than medicine," and then the following part hasn't been translated: "Representatives of the European Monitors have been visiting us and they like us. They have grown to like us." So it is that part that has not been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I just wanted to put that in. So now it would appear that you did have access to this gentleman at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm a just bit confused here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That bit that was read out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right, that you met --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is not in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not in the English version.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry but -- it wasn't translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It wasn't translated. It's nothing to do with you.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But over here they're saying that they met with the European Monitors. "Representatives of the European Monitors have been visiting us, and they like us." In other words -- and this is visiting us. It seems that on more than one occasion.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And they like us, which I think obviously that goes without saying that anybody who probably meets you likes you, but it would seem to me from this you had visits or contacts with the doctor at this particular time.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware of these efforts that he was making and the content of this document?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, have I seen this document before? Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, no, not whether you've seen the document. Are you aware of the contents in the document? In other words, that he was making these efforts trying to get food during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes or no. No, I wasn't aware of it, but I'm not surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. And nothing in this document here -- he refers to the Chetniks, nothing about the HVO at this time denying him access to food or access to resources or any of that stuff. I mean, you read it?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there's nothing in there about that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's nothing there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that concludes my cross-examination, Mr. Lane. Thank you very much. You've been most cooperative. I apologise for the friction in the courtroom. I assure you it's nothing personal.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your courtesy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's almost noon now. It would be best to have our 20-minute break now and we'll resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we begin, Mr. President, over the break when things cooled down a little bit and having consulted with my colleagues as well who took me to task, I wish to extend an apology to Mr. Stringer. It was my intention to offend him. It was an attempt at levity, which obviously didn't work. I understand that we are in a -- I understand that we are in a very important Tribunal, but it -- I didn't mean to demean the process or to disrespect Mr. Stringer. I just merely wanted to lighten up the situation. Obviously it was bad humour on my part and I stand corrected. I apologise if I offended Mr. Stringer, and I apologise to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That closes the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. Could we please provide the Judges with my binder of documents. As far as I have been told, the Prosecution and the witness also have the documents. Mr. Lane, I'd like to clarify certain things. I'd like to see what kind of information you had at the time that you arrived in Herzegovina. As far as your testimony is concerned, your testimony today, and this is something that you also addressed in the course of the statement that you gave to the Prosecution, well, you mentioned your conversations with people in the field, and you said that as a result of those conversations you came to the conclusion that the Republic of Croatia had significant political and military influence on the Croats in Herzegovina. Could you please tell me whether prior arriving in that area you had information of any kind about the relationships between the various regions and about the influence exerted by other states? And what I have in mind primarily are the relationships in the former Yugoslavia. So what sort of influence did other republics have in relation to the territory you were in, or were you aware at the time that the socialist regime in Yugoslavia, many inhabitants, Muslims and Croats, were, in educational and economic terms, oriented towards Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question, Counsel, specifically had I any information before I arrived in the mission area, I had no information on what you've asked me. I had no background knowledge of what you just laid down there, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you think it might be useful for -- for you if you had known that in geographical terms that area was very much linked to Croatia and to Zagreb? Would such information be useful to the conclusions that you drew with regard to the links between the Croats from that area to the Republic of Croatia and Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of the ECMM and their decision to redeploy monitors back into Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was a hasty decision, as I've said, and the preparation that we were given before going into Herzegovina was most definitely insufficient. To answer your question directly would it have been useful, it would have been of tremendous assistance for me and my monitors to have been given a detailed and complete brief on that region of the world. There's no argument about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Although you have said that you knew nothing about that, I'll put this question to you nevertheless. At a subsequent time when you returned from Bosnia, or perhaps while you were still there, did you receive any information according to which prior to the war, at the time of the former Yugoslavia, Croats, Serbs, and Muslims from the Banja Luka region would usually go to Zagreb for professional purposes, and they would usually study in Zagreb. Have you ever heard about such a thing?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that specific example you've given me here, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll just provide you with one more example. Have you ever heard anything about the fact that -- well, for example, the Muslims from the Bihac area, from the wider Bihac area, an area in which even before the war the population was almost 98 per cent Muslim, had more links to Zagreb and Slovenia because of the proximity, and did you hear anything about the fact that that also had an influence on the future conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Have you ever heard anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's important to say that the lack of such information that you weren't provided with because of the sudden decision about sending you on mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina, it's important to say that as a result of such a lack of information it was possible to draw erroneous conclusions. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've said on a number of occasions I'm -- I'm an experienced overseas officer in a number of theatres around the world, and I've said yesterday that my number one drive and concern is for the well-being of people, no matter where they come from. I absolutely agree I would have liked more information before I went in there. Absolutely, that's definite. But that wasn't possible. But I just draw your attention to one thing. When I was in Gornji Vakuf, the local commanders, the Muslim and Croat commanders of the opposing sides before the war were the best of friends and in fact played on the same soccer team together. My -- my ambition and my -- and my energy was directed at getting those people back talking again around the table, to try to bring them back to some normality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Lane, I asked you about these relationships before the war in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the area of Herzegovina because through your answers you also provided certain political assessments, and it's quite clear to me that you were a soldier and that you attempted to carry out your tasks as a soldier, to the best of your ability. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- it's an interesting comment. The ECM mission -- ECMM mission is a mixture of diplomatic and military, and as you point correctly, you point I'm a military officer, but I'd also like to point out that at the end of my mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina, on my report for my conduct for the six months, the ambassador in Zagreb pointed out that I had very good diplomatic skills, which, he's an expert in that area, I have to accept.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I wasn't referring to the entire mission but only to what you stated had been your experience. It's quite clear to me that the mission also had as its objective an assessment of the political and military situation, but we'll now move on to Mostar. My colleague Mr. Karnavas put a series of questions to you and has therefore facilitated this part of my cross-examination for me, but I'll just focus on some areas that I believe have not yet been clarified. You said that you went to Eastern Mostar about seven days after your arrival in Siroki Brijeg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And today we established that you were aware of the fact that the staff of the 4th Corps of the ABiH was in Western Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever meet -- or, rather, did you know that members of the ABiH would come -- or would go to the headquarters in Western Mostar and would leave Eastern Mostar to do so?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I know? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We could see through Mr. Karnavas's cross-examination that the inhabitants would move from the east to the west of Mostar and vice versa because there were no borders in the town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no borders in the town, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, you said at that Mr. Bozic was surprised when you told him that you had been to East Mostar. If it was quite normal for members of the ABiH to go from one side of the town to the other and for inhabitants of the town to go from one side to the other, in that case why would he object to the fact that you also went to Eastern Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the same question I asked Mr. Bozic. But when you refer to a normal situation, the situation on East Mostar, I think as I pointed out in cross-examination, was not normal. But to answer your direct question, I don't know why Mr. Bozic was unhappy with me being in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When we discuss Eastern Mostar -- well, you say the situation wasn't normal there, and we both agree on that. At the time of your stay in that area, that situation was a result of the war between the HVO -- or it was a result of the war between the HVO and the ABiH against the Serbs in the summer of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the tension that I experienced in East Mostar was as a result of the tension between the Armija and the HVO. That's where the tension was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I don't want to be unpleasant, sir. I know you have mentioned the tension, but I'd be grateful if you could just answer my questions. I have nothing against you providing additional comments. I'm referring now to the objective situation. I'm referring to the situation in Eastern Mostar. I'm referring to the state of the buildings, the water supply. The sort of conditions the people were living in. Those were the results -- or that was the result of the war with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When we refer to this situation that the inhabitants lived in, the inhabitants in Eastern Mostar, well, I'm saying the inhabitants or the citizens. Were you aware of the fact that in the eastern part of Mostar there were both Serbs, Muslims, and Croats at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So when we refer to the conditions in which they lived, we have already been told that you received information from Mr. Pasalic about the water supply situation, and that's a fairly important matter for the life of a town. So at that time were you aware of the fact that apart from the military authorities, apart from the ABiH, there were civilian authorities that were functioning on the eastern side of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with the representatives of the civilian authorities in Eastern Mostar and, if so, did you ask them about what they had done to facilitate the lives of the citizens of Eastern Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had discussions with representatives, civilian representatives, of the population of eastern -- Eastern Mostar, in particular medical representatives in relation to hospitals, clinics, medicines, and food.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, we'll come to the subject of hospitals, but I'm asking you the following: The civilian authorities in Eastern Mostar according to the documents that you've been shown in the courtroom existed at the time that you were in the area. Isn't that correct? I'll be quite free to put this in a colloquial manner. The civilian authorities were the Muslim civilian authorities. Did you ever meet representatives of those authorities? Did you meet the people who were responsible for the citizens there in the western part of Mostar you met various representatives of the political -- of the military and of the civilian authorities. On the eastern side of Mostar you noticed that the situation was very difficult, but apart from speaking to Mr. Pasalic, did you try to speak to anyone who was a member of the civilian authorities? Did you ask them what they had done?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said to you, I spoke to many, many people, but also not just me. My monitors also, as I said, spent some time in Eastern Mostar. So we spoke to many, many people over there who had different jobs and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Whom did you speak to? If you spoke to members of the civilian authorities, I would then expect you to know at least one name, because you knew the names of the people you spoke to in Western Mostar.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately I cannot remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Your testimony shows that in a certain sense you believed when you had contact with representatives of the authorities in the west you -- you believed they were responsible for the situation in Eastern Mostar. My question is as follows: Do you know that at the time of the attack launched by the Serbian army numerous Muslims and Croats from Eastern Mostar and from Herzegovina as a whole took refuge in Western Mostar, in flats, for example, that had been abandoned by Serbs? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that many of them stayed on in those flats in Western Mostar later on either because it was not possible for them to return to Eastern Mostar or because the living conditions in that part of Mostar were better than the conditions in the eastern part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that the authorities in Western Mostar had in fact attempted to shelter all those displaced individuals? They had attempted to provide them with everything that they needed for their daily lives, and this related to thousands of displaced Muslims and Croats, tens of thousands of Muslims and Croats, and it required substantial resources. Were you aware of this at all?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that the HVO authorities, both the military and civilian authorities, from the very beginning of the conflict with the Serbs, provided material resources? They provided food, other supplies, weapons, to the ABiH at the time that you were there? To be more specific, they provided these supplies to the 4th Corps, and I believe Mr. Pasalic could have provided you with examples of such aid. When you spoke to representatives of the 4th Corps and representatives of the civilian authorities whom you cannot identify, in the course of your conversations with these representatives did you find out anything about this in did you know that prior to your arrival such aid was provided by the HVO and such aid continued after you had left? Did anyone ever tell you anything about this?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically are you saying that the HVO provided weapons and military assets to the Armija while I was there? Is that the question? That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, that too.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That too. No. The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that the Republic of Croatia throughout the entire period, I'm referring to the period prior to your arrival, and I'm referring to the period during your stay there and after you had left, do you know that the Republic of Croatia aided the citizens of Eastern Mostar and in your time the citizens of Mostar as a whole? Did you know anything about the aid provided by Croatia to the territory that you were in regardless of whether that territory was under the HVO or the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my many travels and movement around the area I saw, personally, no sign of aid coming from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica, I would like to draw your attention to the fact and also to Mr. Lane's attention that the French translation is very much lagging behind of your -- your questions and answers, so please try to -- to look into that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll bear that in mind, but I was under the impression that I was speaking exceptionally slowly, but I will slow down even more.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, did you know that -- well, you said that you were often in Split, so we can take Split as an example, but did you know that in Croatia and in particular in Split there were numerous humanitarian organisations? For example, Muslim humanitarian organisations such as Merhamet, the Red Crescent. Were you aware of the fact that at the time that you were in the area they provided the Muslim inhabitants of Herzegovina with aid?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- I accept what you're saying. They obviously provided some inhabitants with aid, but there were many Muslim inhabitants in Herzegovina that were not in receipt of aid from these organisations or any other organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know that, for instance, in Split there was a Crisis Staff, a military Crisis Staff, for Bosnia and Herzegovina, for the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, before your arrival, during your tour of duty, and after you had left?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify this for me so I can answer, what was the structure? Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll show you a document. Maybe that will help you to see what kind of structure it is. But before that, let's go back to the distribution that you mentioned. You said that you knew that there were humanitarian organisations but that their aid didn't reach everyone. Can one conclude from this that the distribution of aid which went to the Muslim population was not done properly perhaps? Perhaps it was the BiH army that took most of the aid so that the smaller part was left for the civilian population, and that is why it didn't reach anyone. Did you have any information along those lines?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the cases that I have pointed out yesterday, Stolac, Posusje, Gradska, and other areas, the solution for the supply of humanitarian aid for these people lay in the region in that, as I've also pointed out there was sufficient food in the area, humanitarian aid, for these people. I also mentioned that I was aware, being an Irish man, that the Irish people had sent substantial amount of humanitarian aid to Medjugorje to relieve desperate situations. So in answer to your question, for these areas there was sufficient food in the area, or humanitarian aid, to assist these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm afraid you haven't answered my question again. I'm talking about the distribution of humanitarian aid that did reach the Muslims coming from the UNHCR to Eastern Mostar who -- that reached from Merhamet and was intended for Eastern Mostar. My question was whether you were aware of the way in which that humanitarian aid was distributed. Did you have any information about the distribution?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that there was very serious difficulties in the transportation of humanitarian aid into Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you contact the UNHCR to see what kind of difficulties they were contending with, and did you receive any information from them about the arrival of humanitarian aid for the whole region? And if you did, who did you speak to in the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man I spoke to was a Mr. -- Mr. Savage [phoen], who was the head of the operations for the UNHCR in Metkovic, a former retired Irish army officer. So I spoke to him about humanitarian aid, relief for Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, excuse me. It's a follow-up to the questions you have asked. The witness has spoken about Irish humanitarian aid, him being an Irishman. Perhaps you could ask him how Irish aid was transported and distributed to the population. Perhaps that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll just convey your question to the witness, that is, whether he knows how this aid was distributed, the aid coming from Ireland. I wish to express the greatest gratitude to Ireland. A large number of countries -- other countries sent aid to Bosnia and Herzegovina through UNHCR, and it was distributed according to a certain schedule both to members of the Muslim ethnicity and the Croat ethnicity. But let's hear what the witness knows about the Irish aid and its distribution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware, due to the close relationship between the Irish people and the -- the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that significant humanitarian aid was channeled into Herzegovina in the period of time that I was there with the ECMM. A lot of this aid went to Medjugorje, again because of the close relationship between the Catholic church in Ireland and -- and Herzegovina. But I am also aware through personal experience that this aid was not distributed equally as you describe between Croats and Muslims. In fact, I pointed out yesterday that I went to Medjugorje to ask for some assistance, and I specifically mentioned the Irish aid that came into Medjugorje, and assistance was not forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of the fact that this aid from Medjugorje was distributed to the population of Western Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware, as I pointed out, that when I looked for aid to assist people who required it, and the word is "urgently," from Medjugorje, I did not receive this aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you a concrete question. You didn't receive aid, but do you know that that aid was distributed to the citizens of Western Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will accept what you say, but I will also point out that for the people I required aid for, I did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If we accept what I'm saying, then you agree that it was distributed to the citizens of the Western Mostar. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm accepting what you say, but I'm also pointing out to you that when I looked for aid myself for specific targets, I did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, you have said this for the fifth time, but let me ask you for a second time. Was Western Mostar inhabited by both Muslims and Croats, something we have already established? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Will you now look at my pink binder. We're making very slow progress. I'll just show you a couple of documents. 2D 00546. It is the fourth document from the top. That should help you to find it. This is a list. We won't dwell on it for long, but look at the original or the translation. This Crisis Staff, there's a stamp that says: "Crisis Staff for Bosnia and Herzegovina, Split," and the signature says: "Commander of the crisis military staff, Mehmed Malkoc. My question to you was about the Crisis Staff in Split for Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether you know about it, which we see from this document took care of those seriously wounded of the ABiH and the HVO in 1992, and here we have a list of 154 such wounded persons who were cared for in Croatia. Those from number 19 to 23 were sent to Iran. We have the names, and we can see that there are both Muslim and Christian names there. My question is were you aware of this particular action that was taken, though there are many such documents, this activity that took place in the territory of the Republic of Croatia during 1992? Were you aware of it? Did you know that Croatia took care of a large number of wounded, including members of the ABiH and Muslim civilians in 1992 and the beginning of 1993 when you were there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me move briefly to the question of hospitals now. When you were talking about the hospital in Eastern Mostar, were you able to establish whether it was really a hospital or an infirmary? Because it was much later in May that the hospital was established in Eastern Mostar, because all the citizens of Mostar were treated in a hospital located in Western Mostar. So when you're talking about a hospital and the shortage of medicines, were you referring to hospitals or to these infirmaries? I'm sure you're aware of the difference.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In discussions I had with the relevant people in East Mostar, they referred to the buildings as hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And what is your opinion? When you went inside did these appear to you to be hospitals or infirmaries?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you define an infirmary as something smaller than a hospital, I would agree that maybe the term "infirmary" was more applicable than hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you have any information to the effect that medical aid and medical equipment and that even certain patients from Eastern Mostar and Stolac when you were there were treated in Croatia? We are talking about members of both the Armija and Muslims who were treated in Croatia and received medical aid from Croatia, among others.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No information.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll come to this document used by my colleague in which Mr. Kapic, whom you had contact with, speaks of this, speaks of the large number of those whom he had operated on during the conflict with the Serbs, and I'm talking about document 1D - you don't have to look for it - 01053. He operated on a large number of patients, whereas some were sent to Metkovic and Split where it was safer. But your answer is that you had no information about that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the particular document you refer to, 1D 01053, I would like to match that with the report that the Prosecution gave yesterday into the article in the newspaper on the same hospital and the conditions in the hospital at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: With your permission, I had planned to focus on this. We will be moving on to Stolac now, so I'll be glad to discuss the difference between the newspaper article and what Mr. Kapic says in his letter, but let us first see about the way in which and the time when you went to Stolac for the first time. Can you remember when the European mission went to the hospital in Stolac for the first time? You said it was November 1992. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was this the beginning of November 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said to you dates are difficult, but however in Mr. Kapic's letter dated the 28th of November, 1992, as pointed out by Mr. Prlic he mentions the presence of EU representatives in the hospital. So it was obviously before the 28th. And he refers to a number of visits. So I'd say it's possibly early November.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, since you yourself said that there were quite a number of check-points among others on the road from Mostar to Stolac, there were HVO check-points, how did you travel? Did you need a pass? And what was the actual procedure for obtaining such pass?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, due to the fact that ECMM had freedom of movement in the area, when we'd arrive at a check-point we would be invariably brought straight through. Subsequent to that, we had to obtain a special pass to go into -- into Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But technically speaking, who did you ask this pass from and how did you obtain it?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I -- sorry. From what I remember, the pass was obtained from the HVO headquarters in Mostar. That I can -- I cannot be 100 per cent sure, except we had to get a special pass.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will show you another document, a series of documents. Can you perhaps recall, let me ask you this, in the period of the beginning of November until the end of December 1992, how many times roughly did representatives of your mission or you yourself visit this hospital in Stolac? I'm asking you this because during your examination, you said that from a certain point in time you had difficulty in going there. So I'm asking you to the best of your recollection how many times did you go there and what kind of problems did you have in going there and contacting those people?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What dates? Give me the dates again. From the start of November to the end of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you've said that you went there for the first time at the beginning of November. Now, I'm asking you up until the end of the year, do you remember how many times you went there, you and members of your mission? How many times did you visit that hospital?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say I was there personally on three occasions, and the members of my mission, other monitors, would have been there maybe seven or eight times in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you asked for permission to go to Stolac, on those requests did you indicate that you wanted to visit the hospital in Stolac, and were you given such permits to pass through the check-points?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: After some discussion with the authorities we received the -- the special permits to pass through. But remember that part of the operational activity of ECMM in the area was freedom of movement. We should not have had to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, was Stolac in the war zone in those days when you went to Stolac?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you point out, Stolac was more or less on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the article by the journalist, as well as in the letter that we saw a moment ago shown to you by Mr. Karnavas, it says that Stolac was being shelled on a daily basis from Serb positions. You don't have to read it. Trust me. You say more or less was that a war zone. You're a soldier, I am not. If there are shooting three times a day from Serb positions and a return of fire from Stolac, was that a war zone?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was there an operation ongoing there, a military operation? Thank you. Then you said after some discussion with the authorities regarding the visit to Stolac. Which authorities in Stolac, the official authorities in Stolac or the authorities in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What was the difficulty of obtaining the pass? I see, Mostar. I will show you now in my binder a series of documents and I believe we can cover them quickly to see how things evolved in Mostar. Would you please look at document 2D 00458. It is the sixth document from the top?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 458. That will help you find it. This is a request addressed to Mr. Bruno Stojic. I have taken it because we have this request. This is an error in the e-court. It's an error in the e-court. You have a hard copy with you. I'll take care that this doesn't happen again. You have this request addressed to Mr. Stojic by your colleague for a list of members who wish to visit Stolac. Do you remember that similar -- such similar requests were addressed? You have it in the original, handwritten by your colleague. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Will you please now look at 2D 00549, again in my binder. It is the seventh from the top.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would this be one such authorisation given on the 25th of January? And we see that the gentleman from the European Union mission and a list of names are allowed to travel from Mostar to Stolac. And it also says that all HVO members situated along the route are obliged to give the above-named gentlemen all necessary assistance. And it says that this authorisation is valid from January 25th to January 31st, 1993. Is that right? I will skip over some documents because I don't have time. 2D 00551. It is the ninth from the top in your binder. According to our documents, this would be probably the first date when you -- this time it is by you, the request for authorisation. Have you found it? 2D 00551?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you remember this request? And it says that you asked for it. Can you remember whether this perhaps was your first visit to the hospital in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So there -- there was a visit before this?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Let me just make a list of documents. 2D 00559. This is authorisation dated the 20th of November. Then we have 2D 00560, authorisation dated the 24th of November. And on all these authorisations it is explicitly stated that it is requested for the purpose of visiting the hospital in Stolac. Next document 2D 00561 dated the 30th of November, 1992, again your request and the authorisation. 2D 00562, this is towards the end of my binder. You can leaf through it, the whole of it. And the authorisation is dated the 10th of December. 2D 00550, authorisation dated the 15th of December. 2D 00563, an authorisation dated the 19th of December. And the last one, 2D 00 - the last document in the binder - 564, an authorisation dated the 28th of December. Sir, if there were some initial difficulties regarding your visit to Stolac, can you confirm that you asked for these authorisations and received them? And Mr. Stojic who signed all these documents made an effort to make sure that you receive a proper authorisation to visit Stolac whenever you asked for such an authorisation?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: These permits are accurate and, as you say, signed by Mr. Stojic. The point I made at the very beginning was ECMM vehicles had freedom of movement in the area and did not require permits.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to kindly ask you to answer my questions. I asked you whether this was a war zone. I don't want to enter into a dispute with you as to who may have been transported with you to the war zone. Could members of the Serb army have been in your vehicle? What was it the duty of any army in a war zone to check who was entering a war zone? If with these authorisation you were able to enter the municipality of Stolac, my question is whether that is so, whether you had any difficulty with the authorities in Mostar to obtain these authorisations and to reach your destination? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to that is whether you have a special pass or not will not make you more safe or less safe in a war zone. As we approached those check-points on every occasion our vehicles were stopped and the personnel inside were checked. We carried our own identity, our own white uniform as we were referred to earlier on. So the question of carrying Serb personnel in our vehicles, really it's not a serious proposition.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, unfortunately I don't have enough time. I have to deal with another three documents with you. But you're a soldier, and you know perfectly well as I do, as does anyone who was in the war zone, and I was there, too, that it was vehicles, even of the UNHCR, that Mujahedin travelled in Central Bosnia, that your vehicles were captured and that enemy soldiers used your vehicles in certain areas. All I wanted to say was that my own layman experience, as compared to your military experience, certainly confirms that these type of checks were necessary in a war zone. That's all I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you're saying that the issue of a special pass is important in a war zone for particular security reasons, and I'm just saying to you as you pointed out that I am a soldier with a lot of experience. There was no requirement for our vehicles to have these special passes. It was contrary to the agreement set down with the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, let's move on, because we obviously won't manage to agree on this subject. It's for the Trial Chamber to make a decision. When you received these passes did you have any problems in access?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What do you mean yes?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our vehicles were stopped. They were --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You asked me --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, I'll withdraw the question, because I see that you insist on repeating something that's already been recorded in the transcript. Let's have a look at the Prosecution document P 10289. It's a newspaper article. P 10289. It's in the Prosecution's binder. Does the witness have that binder? If not, could someone provide him with the binder, or I can provide him with the binder.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You have it. Fine. P 10 ... On the first page of the article it says that the Serbs shelled the local hospitals. There's no dispute about the fact that the damage to the hospital was as a result of the Serbian shelling; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Here it says that at about 120 individuals, prior to the 18th of December when the journalist was there, it says that there were about -- it says that there were about 120 individuals in the hospital, Serbs, Muslims and Croats. He counted the patients and the members of staff as well. On the second page -- you've probably read this article, but please let's have a look at the information that concerns whom the journalist spoke to. Its it says Obrat Kapor, and then it says Kemo Medar, Huso Ratkusic. It says the first person was a Serb, the second was a Muslims. Huso Ratkusic certainly wasn't a Croat. And it also mentions Dr. Kapic. It also mentions military operations conducted in the area, and it says when one curious monitor of the EC asked to travel to Stolac the local Croatian commander insisted on the fact that the hospital there had been closed down a long time ago. The Croats had been forced to admit their mistake only once the representative of the European Community entered the premises. The journalist received this information from you, from you personally or from your mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The journalist received this information from speaking to Mr. Kapic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The penultimate paragraph says: "Food from the high commission of the UN for refugees finally arrived, but the Croats requested special passes for representatives of international humanitarian organisations, and they said that their visits could soon be brought to an end." Who provided the journalist with this information? Do you know? Was it Mr. Kapic again?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea where he got that information from.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, have a look at 2D 00547. This is my document. It's in the pink binder, not in the Prosecution binder. 2D 00547. I'm interested in the fifth line from above -- the fifth document from the top. I apologise. Can you tell me when you have you've found the document? There's the translation after that document. Of it's a list. I'd like to go through it to see whether we could determine whether -- to determine certain matters. The document doesn't have a date. It doesn't bear a signature, but we have the staff members of the hospital enumerated here. Mehmed Kapic, Mr. Mehmed Kapic is under number 1, the former head of the hospital. And then we have president of Merhamet. Did Mr. Kapic ever tell you that he was also the president of the Merhamet charity at the time when you had contact with him?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And, sir, did you ever speak to him about whether Merhamet sent any aid to him? Did he receive any aid through the Merhamet charity?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a European Commission or community monitoring mission point of view, there was not enough humanitarian aid getting through to Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, you are deliberately avoiding answering my question. My question was very specific. Did you know certain things? Did you ask him about is this? Did Merhamet send humanitarian aid in -- we've had a member of the Merhamet charity appear here, and at the time and subsequently they went to Split. So all I want to know under number 35 we also have the name of the vice-president of Merhamet in this list. So did you have any information that you received from him according to which he received aid from the Merhamet charity?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no information.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, we have 36 staff members here. I performed analysis. I examined all the staff members, and according to the information I have we can see from this list that these individuals were there at the time that you were in -- were visiting the area. It says with regard to some individuals that they found employment after the liberation. They mean after the occupation of the Serbs, and then it says the individuals under 17 and 18 went to the ABiH. But amongst these individuals -- well, it's -- I could say that there are at least six individuals who have Christian names. Can you make a distinction between Christian and Muslim names? Are you able to do so?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I ask you, what is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I have already said that the document does not have a date. I received the document in this form. But I am trying to see whether this is the situation that prevailed when you were in the area. Are you able to make a distinction between Muslim and Croat names? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you have already used you have one hour. Have you been granted any additional time?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have just one more document I would like to show the witness, and I believe that one of my colleagues will allow me a little extra time, or perhaps I may make use of some of the time that Mr. Karnavas did not use up. I only require another five minutes. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas used all his time up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I'll be granted some time from the other Defence teams. If I may only have another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, could you have a look at the page that list the names of patients. It's the second page. In article the names Obrat Kapor are mentioned, Kemo Medar, these people he spoke to and also Huso Ratkusic. Have a look at the name under number 22. It says Kapor. We don't have the first name. And have a look at number 19, Huso Ratkusic, and number 20, Kemo Medar. These people are listed as patients at the time that you were there, at the time your journalist was there too. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I have an objection because it's clear we don't have the time frame of the document I think it's incorrect for counsel to suggest that these people were patients in the hospital at the time that the witness and the journalist was there, which is what was just said. So I know that we all have to take the documents in the way they come to us, and unfortunately this one doesn't have a date. So I think it's of very limited use to any of us in terms of its utility.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I just asked the witness -- we identified the names in P 10289, a Prosecution document. We identified the names. These are the three names of patients that the journalist spoke to, the journalist who wrote an article on the 18th of December, 1992, and these are the three names I pointed out in the list of patients. I'm asking the witness if he would accept these are the patients referred to in the article, and can he recognise other names apart from the name of Dr. Kapic in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with these people? Can you recognise any of the names here or not? If not, we'll move on. I'm asking you this because in these lists -- in this list of patients and employees you can see that at least half of them are both Croats or Serbs in relation to Muslims. Among the patients there's almost an identical number of Muslims, Croats, and Serbs. Did you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information, I mean, I cannot comment on this document because I don't know what date, when it is, where it came from. I can't comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you confirm that there were Serbs, Croats, and Muslims in that hospital?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And, sir, finally, with regard to the extent the HVO aided the ABiH you said that you knew nothing about that. Have a look at the first document in my binder 2D 00229. It is marked in a particular way. It's already been admitted. When you find the document, have a look at the document dated the 26th of February, 1993. It was signed by Arif Pasalic. There's no doubt about that. Item 2 concerns the period during which you were there. This is what Pasalic -- Mr. Pasalic says about the relationships with the HVO: "Mr. Orucevic Safet successfully performed major jobs up until now with regard to the entrance of goods with the HVO." I'm referring to this sentence here, this sentence alone, but this sentence shows that Mr. Arif Pasalic, on the 26th of February, 1993, expressed his satisfaction with cooperation with the HVO when it comes to the delivery of goods to the area in which the 4th Corps was present. Did you know anything about that? Did the article mention anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm trying to read this and you're talking at the same time. So maybe if you just give me a minute or two to read the document if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I have no more time left. I don't want to deceive you. The document has been admitted into evidence. I asked you, just like the Prosecution asked you, about certain parts of the document. In the case of the Mujahedin, you said that with regard to a certain segment of the document you hadn't heard about that. So I'm just referring to this sentence, this sentence written by Mr. Pasalic in which he said that he was satisfied with cooperation with the HVO when it came to the delivery of goods, and I'm asking you whether he ever mentioned this cooperation when you spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your direct question did he ever mention it to me, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. That concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, I would like to go back to the passes for the European mission in order to visit the hospital in Stolac. When examining all the documents presented by the Defence, I came to the following conclusion: The vehicles that you used to move around had registration number with the letters EUR and a number. For example, only the 13th of November, you had authorisation for a Mercedes -- two Mercedes, and the numbers were 8715 and 7886. You were to be escorted by the military police on that occasion. So there were vehicles with the registration numbers that belonged to the European mission, and then I have found out that other forms of authorisation were provided on behalf of the European Union. Have a look at document 560 where three individuals -- or, rather, two individuals are mentioned, two individuals and a translator, and the vehicle had a French registration number. So on that day was it also part of the European mission? Could you explain that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did notice that as I went through the different authorisations. I -- no, I'm not aware of what that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not aware of it, Your Honour. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have a look at document 562. It's another authorisation. It bears your name on it. And I noticed that there are apparently two vehicles here, one of which has a registration number in Paris or is registered in Paris. How is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. That's document 2D 561, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 562. That's the last document. It's an authorisation for the 10th of December, an authorisation yet again to visit the Stolac Hospital. I was wondering whether when the European mission visited these places you used resources from the outside too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What remains for the Defence now for tomorrow? I believe that we have the Petkovic Defence, the Praljak Defence. Is that correct? Ms. Alaburic -- yes, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given that I am adhering to what I'm allowed to do, although the commandant says he doesn't like maps, but I do, I think they're very important, I believe they're important in order to see what the actual facts are on the basis of which we can draw conclusions, but I would like to use maps to put some specific questions, especially since my counsel, Mr. Kovacic, is ill. I asked him to appear in the courtroom today. I thought that I would have time to commence with my question today, but if I may, I would like to start first to establish the location of certain things, establish certain numbers, establish certain facts. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you will be the first to start tomorrow, and you will be followed by Ms. Alaburic; is that correct? And I believe that Mr. Coric gave his time to Mr. Karnavas. And that is also the case for Mr. Pusic. So that's our schedule for tomorrow. Witness, as you can see, you'll be back tomorrow. We'll be sitting in the afternoon tomorrow. We switched courtrooms today, but tomorrow we will be sitting at 2.15. It's almost time to adjourn, so I do thank you, and I will see you all tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
